wedge.question: My schedule is filling up. Is it time to raise prices?

copy.page_title: Salon pricing decision — three options compared

world_verdict_labels.C: A 5% rise plus shifting the mix

copy.headline: Your diary is {shock}% busier. Is it time to raise prices?
copy.hero_lede: We compared three decisions using the same model of your salon and the same assumptions. Only the decision changes between them — so the differences come from the decision, not from different guesses.

sens_help.low: A loyal client base who book with you personally.
sens_help.central: Our judgement for an appointment business with real switching costs.
sens_help.high: Stress case: clients who treat it as a commodity and shop on price.

copy.capacity_note: Because your diary has a ceiling, some of the {unit} a price rise costs you were being turned away anyway. That is why raising prices costs less here than the price sensitivity on its own suggests.
copy.c_card_note: Depends on three of our assumptions: how much shifting the mix cuts your {cost} (about {red} points here), how much it lifts the average ticket, and how many {unit} leave with the discounts ({loss}%). None is calibrated to your business yet.
copy.chart_title: Cash in the bank under each decision
copy.chart_lede: Clients on a six-week cycle only meet a new price at their next visit, so the reaction arrives over a couple of weeks rather than at once.
copy.next_measurement: Raise the price of one service, or for new clients only, and count rebookings for six weeks. That is a direct measurement of the one number this decision hangs on — and for a salon there is no published figure to fall back on, so your own test is worth more here than in any other trade.
copy.sources_note: On price sensitivity: we found no published elasticity for personal-care services that could be used honestly. Every setting on that control is our judgement. The retail studies listed are only the reference points our range was positioned against — they measure shoppers switching brands, not clients changing salon.
limits_does_not: Predict the future or guarantee an outcome.
Model hiring, longer opening hours or a second chair.
Model competitors, word of mouth or reputation.
Know your clients' price sensitivity — there is no published figure, so your own test is the only real evidence.

variables.label: Demand for appointments in your area

interventions.label: Raise service prices
interventions.description: Adds the given number of percentage points to the average service price for the whole horizon. Magnitude is the price increase in percent.

interventions.label: Shift the diary toward higher-margin services
interventions.description: Reduces discounting and moves slots toward services that earn more per appointment. Magnitude is the reduction in variable cost per appointment, in percentage points of today's cost; it also lifts the average price slightly because the mix is richer, and costs a share of appointments from clients who came for the discounted services. All three ratios are expert assumptions - see the evidence registry.

event.label: Appointments wanted +{shock}%
event.description: Demand for appointments rises and stays at the new level for 90 days.

options.label: Keep prices, serve more
options.headline: Leave prices where they are and fit in as many of the extra appointments as the diary allows.

options.label: Raise prices 10%
options.headline: Raise prices 10% and let demand settle back toward the slots you actually have.

options.label: Raise prices 5% + shift the mix
options.headline: A smaller 5% rise, plus moving the diary toward services that earn more and cutting discounting.

registry_spec.label: How full the diary is today
registry_spec.note: Tested at 75% and 95% as well. This decides how much the capacity ceiling matters: at 95% full, appointments lost to a price rise were largely being turned away anyway.

registry_spec.label: How much busier it has become
Monthly product cost
registry_spec.note: Products and consumables only. Wages are in fixed costs.

registry_spec.label: Monthly fixed costs (incl. wages)
registry_spec.note: Treated as unchanged over 90 days. Over that horizon a salon's staff cost does not move with one more or one fewer appointment, which is why serving extra clients adds little cost and why the capacity ceiling, not the cost, is the binding constraint.

registry_spec.label: Share of appointments on discounted / low-margin services
Price sensitivity of clients
registry_spec.assumption_source: No direct source. bijmolt2005 / tellis1988 are listed only as the retail reference points the range is positioned against.
registry_spec.note: A 1% price rise eventually reduces appointments WANTED by this percentage. Low 0.30 / central 0.60 / high 1.20. NO published elasticity for personal-care services with a usable mean was found, so all three settings are our judgement, not research. They sit below the retail brand-level meta-analyses because changing hairdresser costs a client more than changing brand on a shelf — an argument, not evidence. The high setting exists to test what happens if that argument is wrong.

registry_spec.label: Appointment slots available per day
registry_spec.note: Appointments per day divided by how full the diary is. Held fixed for 90 days: hiring or extending hours is a different decision from the one being compared here.

registry_spec.label: What happens when demand exceeds the slots

value.text: appointments served = the smaller of wanted and available

registry_spec.note: An accounting identity, not a simulated behaviour. Appointments above the ceiling are counted as turned away — which the business itself usually cannot observe, so treat that figure as a model quantity rather than a measurement.

registry_spec.label: How quickly clients react to a price change
registry_spec.note: Clients on a six-week cycle only meet a new price at their next visit, which is why even the fast setting is not immediate.

registry_spec.label: Cost saving from shifting the service mix

value.text: {reduction:g} points off cost per appointment ({mix_effectiveness:.2f} per point of low-margin share)

registry_spec.note: Tested at half and one-and-a-half times this rate.

registry_spec.label: Price gain from a richer mix
registry_spec.note: 0.25 of the cost saving: services that cost more to deliver generally sell for more.

registry_spec.label: Appointments lost from cutting discounts
registry_spec.note: 0.4 of the cost saving, in points of demand: clients who came for the discounted service and will not pay full price.

registry_spec.label: Price rises compared
registry_spec.note: The decisions being compared; fixed by the question.

registry_spec.label: Comparison horizon
registry_spec.note: Long enough for clients on a typical rebooking cycle to meet the new price at least once; short enough that rent and wages can be treated as fixed. Hiring, or opening more hours, is outside it.

registry_spec.label: Average price per appointment
registry_spec.note: Monthly sales divided by monthly appointments.

sweep_labels.utilisation_pct: How full the diary really is
sweep_labels.demand_growth_pct: How much busier it has actually become
sweep_labels.mix_effectiveness: How much shifting the mix really saves

sources.citation: Bijmolt THA, van Heerde HJ, Pieters RGM. New empirical generalizations on the determinants of price elasticity. Journal of Marketing Research. 2005;42(2):141-156.
sources.population: 1,851 price elasticities from 81 studies, predominantly packaged consumer goods in retail scanner data
sources.limitations: Brand-level in supermarket categories with near-perfect substitutes on the same shelf. It measures switching between brands inside a shop, not switching between shops.
sources.transfer: Used as the upper reference point. For a shop it is the 'my customers can buy the identical thing elsewhere' end of the range; for a cafe it is further away still, and the HIGH setting of 1.60 there is a judgement placed between the food category CI top (1.07) and this mean.

sources.citation: Tellis GJ. The price elasticity of selective demand: a meta-analysis of econometric models of sales. Journal of Marketing Research. 1988;25(4):331-341.
sources.population: 367 price elasticities from roughly 220 brands and markets
sources.limitations: Selective (brand-level) demand, largely goods rather than services, and estimated from studies published up to the mid-1980s. Like Bijmolt it measures brand switching, not store switching.
sources.transfer: A second brand-level reference point for the shop wedge, quoted so the range shown is not resting on a single meta-analysis. It does not establish what happens when one shop raises all of its prices at once.

intake_fields.label: Appointments per day
intake_fields.hint: How many you actually do on an average working day.

intake_fields.label: How full is the diary?
intake_fields.hint: Roughly what share of your available appointment slots get booked. 100% means completely full.

intake_fields.label: Monthly product cost
intake_fields.hint: Colour, product, consumables — what you use up per appointment. NOT wages and NOT rent.

intake_fields.label: Monthly fixed costs
intake_fields.hint: Rent, wages, utilities, everything that will not change in the next 90 days.

intake_fields.label: Cash available
intake_fields.hint: What is in the business account today.

intake_fields.label: How much busier?
intake_fields.hint: How much more demand you are seeing than before — enquiries, requests, waiting list.

intake_fields.label: Share on discounted / low-margin services
intake_fields.hint: Roughly what share of appointments are discounted or earn you least. A guess is fine; it is tested as an assumption.

demo.name: Demo salon (fictional)
notes: Fictional. A small salon at a realistic margin, not a composite of any real business.
Staff cost sits in fixed costs: over 90 days it does not move with one more appointment.
At 85% full, roughly 14 slots a day exist and 12 are used.

language.scenario_not_forecast: This is a scenario comparison under stated assumptions, not a forecast.
